topics.title: Data sources
topics.text: Each variable comes from one grid cell of one dataset.
list: ERA5-Land, land cell: air temperature (daily maximum and minimum) and rainfall. Daily, {record.airTemperature.start} to {record.airTemperature.end}.
ERA5, sea cell: wind speed, wave height, wave direction and sea surface temperature. Daily, {record.windSpeed.start} to {record.windSpeed.end}.
Satellite altimetry, grid point nearest 21.125°N, 90.125°W: sea level. Monthly, {record.seaLevel.start} to {record.seaLevel.end}.
HYCOM, one pixel: surface salinity. Daily, {record.salinity.start} to {record.salinity.end}.
HURDAT2 (NOAA National Hurricane Center): storm tracks. Every 6 hours, {storms.start} to {storms.end}.

topics.title: Storm selection
topics.text: Counted in "When storms come": {storms.rule} This gives {storms.total} storms. We study {storms.studied} storms in detail: all passed within 100 km of Sisal and have daily climate data (ERA5 starts in {record.windSpeed.start}; earlier storms are counted, not studied). {storms.notCounted} are studied but not counted: near Sisal they were weaker than tropical storm strength.

topics.title: Storm periods and peaks
topics.text: The box and the dashed line in the anomaly charts are the storm period and the peak date of each studied storm. The team sets them by hand in content/storm-periods.json, from the HURDAT2 track of the storm: the peak is the day the storm was closest to Sisal. The export script copies them to data/events.json.

topics.title: Anomalies
topics.text: An anomaly is a daily value minus the mean of the same calendar day. Baseline: {storms.baseline}. The mean uses an 11-day window around each day and is smoothed over 31 days; no trend is removed. The charts show {storms.windowDays} days before and after the peak date (or the middle of the storm period, if there is no peak date).

topics.title: A typical year
topics.text: For each calendar month: the line is the mean of all daily values of the record, the band runs from the 10th to the 90th percentile of those daily values. Rainfall is the mean monthly total (bars). Sea level has no band: it is the monthly mean relative to the annual mean. Air temperature has one panel for the daily maximum and one for the daily minimum.

topics.title: Change since 1950
topics.text: Annual means, over the record of each variable (years with at least 90% of the days; sea level: all 12 months). The trend is a linear regression of the annual means on the year, per decade (sea level: per year). The ± value is the 95% range of the slope (1.96 times its standard error), p is the p-value of the slope. The trend line is drawn only when p < {trend.pLimit}; otherwise the panel says no significant trend.

topics.title: In detail
topics.text: Per month, the band runs from the lowest to the highest daily value; the line is the 365-day running mean (centred, at least 300 days with data). Sea level shows the monthly anomaly (seasonal cycle removed) and its 12-month running mean, with trends for the whole record and for {seaLevel.periods}. Below, the annual means and trend as in Change since 1950.

topics.title: Wave direction
topics.text: The compass is split into 8 sectors of 45°, centred on N, NE, E and so on. Each day is counted in the sector the waves come from (ERA5 daily mean wave direction), {wave.start} to {wave.end}. The wide wedge is all {wave.all} days. The narrow wedge is the {wave.storm} rough-sea days with a maximum wave height above {wave.threshold} m; these are not only tropical cyclones.

topics.title: Limitations
list: One grid cell per variable, not an area average.
ERA5, ERA5-Land and HYCOM are reanalysis (model) data, not local measurements.
The record periods differ: from {record.airTemperature.start} (air temperature, rainfall), {record.windSpeed.start} (wind, waves, sea surface temperature) and {record.seaLevel.start} (sea level).
Salinity only covers {record.salinity.start} to {record.salinity.end} (one HYCOM model version); later storms have no salinity.
Too few storms ({storms.total} in {storms.start} to {storms.end}) for a trend test.

useCases.title: Map of the storm tracks around your site
Chart of when storms come at your site
Anomaly chart of the weather around one storm
steps: Export the daily ERA5-Land, ERA5 and HYCOM values of the grid cells at your site from Earth Engine as CSV, one file per dataset, with a date column.
Look up your storm in HURDAT2 and add its name, storm period (start, end) and peak date to storm-periods.json.
In loading.py, set FILES to your CSV files. load_series() reads each variable as a complete daily series.
Calculate the anomaly with anomaly() in export_typical_year.py: the daily value minus the baseline. Baseline: {storms.baseline}.
Cut the anomaly {storms.windowDays} days before and after the peak date. export_storms() does this and writes the numbers for all storms.
Draw each variable as a filled line around zero, with the storm period as a box and the peak as a dashed line (chart functions: charts.js).
